title: The cost of discipleship
hook: Dietrich Bonhoeffer warns against cheap grace, grace without discipleship

segments.voice: Yesterday, Barmen, and a few pastors who wrote down who their Lord was. Your line was jesus christ is the one word. What voice asked you for too much loyalty? Day nine hundred forty-nine.

Clearance sale. Everything must go. Grace, forgiveness, comfort, all marked down to nothing, no questions asked. That's roughly the picture a young German pastor painted of his own church. Dietrich Bonhoeffer was a Lutheran, from a church built on the teaching that God's grace is free, a gift nobody can earn. He held to that. And still he said the church had started giving grace away the wrong way, like stock it was trying to clear. He had a name for it. Today, the book where he named it.

Bonhoeffer was teaching young pastors for the Confessing Church, the church that had said no at Barmen, in a small seminary the government would later close. Out of that teaching came a book. In English it's called The Cost of Discipleship. In German it has one word for a title, Nachfolge, which means following after. It opens with two kinds of grace. Cheap grace, he wrote, is grace we hand ourselves. Forgiveness without turning around. Church membership without following. Grace without the cross, without Jesus, a doctrine we nod at and then go on living exactly as before. Costly grace is the other kind. He reached for Jesus's short parable in Matthew. In the King James Bible: "the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field." Notice the joy. The man isn't paying a fine. He's found something worth everything. That's costly grace: still a gift, never earned, but a gift that calls you to follow. Bonhoeffer put it in a pair of phrases that people still repeat: it is costly because it costs a life, and it is grace because it gives a life. Jesus said something close in Luke: "For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost?" Christians have argued about the book ever since. Some hear a needed alarm. Others worry it leans too hard on effort and forgets the comfort of grace. Bonhoeffer himself said later that he could see dangers in it, though he stood by it. What makes it hard to brush off is what he did next. He kept following, right into the danger.
screen: `IT COSTS A LIFE, IT GIVES A LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the costly good thing. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one good thing you already know you should do and keep putting off because it will cost you something. An apology that means admitting you were wrong. A call that will take an hour. Speaking up in a meeting. Giving something you'd rather keep. Don't decide anything yet. Just look at it honestly, and notice what the cost actually is. Then notice whether there's a field with treasure behind it. If you pray, you can bring it to God. The bell holds the time.
Bonhoeffer. The German pastor who wrote The Cost of Discipleship, warning against cheap grace that asks nothing and changes nothing.
Your line: not cheap grace. Today, do the costly good thing you pictured, or one honest step toward it. Day nine hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: The Cost of Discipleship is read in church study groups and seminaries across denominations, often alongside the Sermon on the Mount, which takes up much of the book.

myth: Bonhoeffer taught that grace must be earned
he taught grace is a gift. his warning was against grace that asks nothing and changes nothing.
the German title of the book means following after
in the parable, the man sells everything grudgingly
"for joy thereof" he sells all he has. costly grace still comes with joy.

fork.setup: you're a Lutheran pastor. your church preaches that grace is free. what do you warn against?
options: grace handed out with no call to follow.
fork.reveal: Bonhoeffer kept grace free, and warned against cheap grace: forgiveness without turning around, grace without the cross.

original.note: Greek: to follow, the verb in Jesus's call to Matthew, follow me (Matthew 9:9).

trapdoor: what you thought: a book saying faith is expensive.
what it means: a warning against grace that asks nothing, set beside costly grace that is a gift and still calls you to follow.
what a scholar hears: Nachfolge, following after, a Lutheran pastor pressing Luther's free grace against a church at ease with the state.

notes: Bonhoeffer's text is paraphrased throughout (English translations are under copyright). Confirm the paraphrases: cheap grace as 'the grace we bestow on ourselves', 'grace without discipleship, grace without the cross'; costly 'because it costs a man his life', grace 'because it gives a man the only true life'.
The 'clearance sale' image in the hook loosely follows his opening image of grace sold cheaply like goods at market; confirm it is fair.
Matthew 13:44 is cited in his discussion of costly grace (with the pearl and the call of the disciples); confirm.
'Bonhoeffer himself said later that he could see dangers in it, though he stood by it' refers to his prison letter of 21 July 1944; confirm phrasing.
Finkenwalde seminary closed by the Gestapo: said only as 'a small seminary the government would later close'. No dates given (claims rule).
The two readings of the book (needed alarm vs. leaning toward works) are described without ranking.
Editor: overstated 'whose whole message was' and the narrator's claim about his inner conviction softened.
Editor 2: Greek note tied to a specific verse (Matthew 9:9, where the call uses this verb) and that verse added to sources.
